families.name: Graph Neural Network (GNN) Architectures
families.definition: Methods that utilize graph neural networks, such as GCNs and GATs, to learn user and item embeddings by modeling the graph structure of user-item interactions and social relations.

properties.text: GNNs integrate node information and topological structure to learn latent factors for users and items.
Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) model information diffusion processes in graphs to refine user embedding learning.
Graph Attention Networks (GATs) use masked self-attentional layers to assign different weights to neighbors without costly matrix operations.
Simplified GCNs like LightGCN and UltraGCN omit feature transformations and nonlinear activations to accelerate convergence and improve performance.
Dual-channel or multi-channel architectures are used to capture both sequential session information and social influence simultaneously.

limitations.text: Standard GCNs suffer from over-smoothing problems as diffusion depth increases.
Message passing mechanisms in GCNs can slow down training convergence, especially in large-scale systems.
Existing GNN-based methods often fail to consider bias offsets of users or items, such as rating tendencies of fastidious users.
Many models focus primarily on modeling users while neglecting the dynamic changes in item attraction over time.

families.name: High-Order and Hypergraph Models
families.definition: Approaches that extend beyond pairwise relations to model high-order social connections and complex group interactions using hypergraphs or multi-order networks.

properties.text: Hypergraphs provide a natural way to model high-order relations where multiple users interact simultaneously.
Multi-order hypergraph convolutional networks capture implicit social relations and dynamic interest changes over time.
These methods address the limitation of standard social recommenders that only leverage first-order direct neighbors.
High-order social relations, such as friends of friends, are utilized to reveal deeper user preferences.

limitations.text: The potential of hypergraphs for improving social recommendation has been under-explored until recently.
Existing high-order methods often ignore the implicit social relations among users.
Modeling high-order complexity can be computationally expensive if not properly optimized.

families.name: Self-Supervised and Contrastive Learning
families.definition: Techniques that generate supervision signals from the data itself, such as through data augmentation or contrastive tasks, to enhance representation learning in sparse social recommendation scenarios.

properties.text: Self-supervised learning (SSL) helps address data sparsity by learning from unlabeled data.
Contrastive learning identifies properties that distinguish positive from negative samples to resolve popularity bias.
Disentangled contrastive learning frameworks learn distinct representations for collaborative and social domains to model heterogeneous behavior patterns.
Data augmentation methods, such as node or edge dropout, create new data views for self-discrimination based contrastive learning.

limitations.text: Most existing SSL methods build only a bijective mapping between nodes in different views, neglecting self-supervision signals from other nodes.
Directly constructing contrastive learning tasks on different channels may not fully utilize the relationships between channels while maintaining their uniqueness.
Uniform node or edge dropout may not effectively capture the specific structural nuances of social graphs.

families.name: Disentangled and Preference-Aware Models
families.definition: Models that separate user representations into distinct facets, such as collaborative versus social preferences or long-term versus short-term interests, to handle heterogeneous user behaviors.

properties.text: Disentangled models address the limitation of unifying user representations for both user-item interactions and social relations.
Preference-aware networks design specific modules for item aggregation, friend-preference aggregation, and user aggregation.
These methods recognize that socially related users may share preferences only for specific items, not universally.
Multi-facet social relations, such as classmates or colleagues, are explicitly disentangled to encode influence under each facet.

limitations.text: Unifying user representations can impair expressiveness by failing to model heterogeneous behavior patterns in different domains.
Traditional social aggregation models often use highly entangled and complex node representations, which is unreasonable when only part of preferences determines connectivity.
Existing methods often assume social relations are homogeneously applied to all items, which is impractical for diverse user preferences.

families.name: Session-Based Social Recommendation
families.definition: Methods tailored for session-based scenarios that capture short-term, dynamic user preferences by combining sequential session data with social network influences.

properties.text: These models aim to predict the next item in an ongoing session by leveraging both item transition patterns and social influences.
Dual-channel attentive networks are used to combine sequential information and social features to prevent information loss.
Dynamic graph attention networks model context-dependent influencers, where different friends are relied upon for different items.
Efficiency is improved by avoiding the need to process many additional sessions of friends for every prediction.

limitations.text: Existing methods often ignore sequential information, focusing only on graph networks for item transitions.
Modeling entire sessions with invalid or repeatedly clicked items can interfere with recommendation results.
Processing additional sessions of friends to capture social influence can be computationally inefficient.

families.name: Trust and Influence Diffusion Models
families.definition: Frameworks that explicitly model the propagation of social influence and trust, distinguishing between explicit and implicit influences to refine user preference modeling.

properties.text: Neural influence diffusion networks model the social influence diffusion process from the global social network structure.
Models distinguish between local implicit influence on unobserved interpersonal relations and global implicit influence of items.
Adversarial approaches are used to disentangle homophily and influence, which cannot be separated from observational data alone.
Trust-aware variational methods estimate diverse levels of influence among entities rather than assuming equal influence.

limitations.text: Most existing methods focus only on explicit influence on observed social links, ignoring implicit influence.
Social relations are often noisy and indiscriminately used, leading to failure in practice for users with limited neighbors.
It is fundamentally difficult to disentangle homophily and influence from observational data to determine the effect of social inference.

families.name: Heterogeneous and Multi-Relational Graph Models
families.definition: Approaches that handle the complexity of real-world social networks by modeling multiple types of relationships, heterogeneous trust, and diverse interaction patterns.

properties.text: Heterogeneous information diffusion models address the loss of heterogeneity in separate social and interaction graphs.
Multi-relational attention networks use similarity-based mechanisms to solve data sparsity by supplementing with item homogeneous relations.
These models capture heterogeneous trust relations among customers and heterogeneous interactions between customers and products.
Bilateral filtering GCNs address the power-law property of degree distributions to better learn representations for long-tail nodes.

limitations.text: Most existing methods assume only single social relations, ignoring the impact of multifaceted social relations.
Vanilla GCNs with static normalized adjacency matrices have limitations in learning node representations for long-tail nodes due to power-law properties.
Representing social data as two separate graphs (user-user and user-item) leads to a loss of heterogeneity.

families.name: Hyperbolic and Geometric Embedding Methods
families.definition: Techniques that learn user and item representations in non-Euclidean spaces, such as hyperbolic space, to better capture hierarchical structures in social data.

properties.text: Hyperbolic social recommendation aims to learn compact but strong representations that exploit the latent hierarchical property of data.
Hyperbolic geometry naturally reflects heterogeneous degree distributions and strong clustering in complex networks.
These methods overcome the limitations of Euclidean space in exploring latent hierarchical properties.

limitations.text: Existing methods usually learn representations in Euclidean space, which has large limitations for exploring latent hierarchical properties.
The application of hyperbolic geometry in social recommendation is a novel problem with limited prior work.
Social recommender systems consistently fail in practice for users with a very limited number of neighbors in social networks.
There is a lack of in-depth analysis of implicit assumptions in existing GNN-based social recommendation methods.
It remains challenging to simultaneously model the static and dynamic features of users and items while integrating time information and social relations.
The problem of disentangling homophily and influence from observational data to determine the effect of social inference is inherently adversarial and unresolved.
Most existing methods do not fully exploit the multi-type user-item interactive behavior and the underlying cross-relational inter-dependencies.
There is a need for more efficient methods for session-based social recommendation that do not require processing many additional sessions of friends.
The potential of hypergraph structures for modeling high-order social relations in recommendation is still under-explored.
Existing self-supervised learning methods neglect self-supervision signals from nodes other than the bijective mapping pairs.
